name: Gulab Jamun

ingredients.name: Refined oil for frying (or ghee)
ingredients.householdMeasure: about ⅔ cup in a small kadai

equipment: Small kadai or deep small pan for frying: needs about 5 cm depth of oil
Mixing bowl, fork and a sieve (optional)
Wide bowl or lidded container to soak the jamuns in syrup

steps.title: Measure the dry ingredients
steps.text: Put milk powder 30 g (3½ tbsp), maida 8 g (1 tbsp) and a small pinch of baking soda (about 1/16 tsp) in a bowl.
steps.visualCue: A small heap of off-white powder with a few white flecks of flour
steps.cameraCheck: The bowl with the three dry ingredients, and the pinch of soda on a spoon
steps.videoShot: Tablespoon of milk powder dropping into the bowl.
steps.watchOut: Too much baking soda, which makes the jamuns break up or taste bitter; use only a small pinch, not a half teaspoon.

steps.title: Mix the dry ingredients
steps.text: Stir with a fork for 30 seconds, or sift them together.
steps.visualCue: One even colour with no streaks of white flour
steps.cameraCheck: The mixed powder, smooth and lump-free
steps.videoShot: Fork stirring the powder in the bowl.
steps.watchOut: Milk powder lumps; press them against the bowl with the fork and break them up now, or they stay as dry spots in the dough.

steps.title: Add the ghee
steps.text: Add 3 g (¾ tsp) melted ghee and rub it into the powder with your fingertips.
steps.visualCue: The powder looks like fine, slightly damp breadcrumbs that hold a shape when squeezed gently
steps.cameraCheck: Your fingertips rubbing the crumbly mix over the bowl
steps.videoShot: Ghee being drizzled onto the powder and rubbed in.
steps.watchOut: Hot ghee, which can cook the milk powder; let the ghee cool until warm to the touch before adding.

steps.title: Add milk a little at a time
steps.text: Add 1 tbsp (15 ml) milk, mix lightly, then add up to 1 tsp more only if the mix still looks dry.
steps.visualCue: The crumbs start to stick together into a soft, slightly sticky lump
steps.cameraCheck: The dough lump in the bowl
steps.videoShot: A spoon adding milk, then a hand pressing the crumbs into a lump.
steps.watchOut: Too much milk, which makes the dough sticky and the jamuns flat or greasy; if it gets sticky, dust a few pinches of milk powder on it. Too little milk gives cracks, so add milk by the half teaspoon.

steps.title: Bring the dough together without kneading
steps.text: Press and fold it 4-5 times only, then cover and rest it for 5 minutes.
steps.tip: The dough should feel like soft clay. Its softness is what makes the jamun soft.
steps.visualCue: A soft, smooth dough that feels like soft cookie dough and does not stick to your palm
steps.cameraCheck: The finished dough, pressed with a finger to show a soft dent
steps.videoShot: A finger pressing the soft dough, leaving a dent.
steps.watchOut: Kneading hard, which makes the jamuns tough and rubbery; handle it as little as you can. A dry or cracked dough should get one more drop of milk.

steps.title: Start the syrup
steps.text: In a small saucepan put 50 g (4 tbsp) sugar and 75 ml (5 tbsp) water and heat on medium, stirring until the sugar dissolves.
steps.visualCue: The liquid turns from cloudy with crystals to clear
steps.cameraCheck: The clear syrup just before it boils
steps.videoShot: Sugar and water in the pan turning from cloudy to clear.
steps.watchOut: Stirring after the sugar has dissolved and the pot is boiling, which can make sugar crystals form on the sides; stop stirring once it is clear.

steps.title: Finish the syrup
steps.text: Crush 1 cardamom pod, add it and simmer for 3-4 minutes, add 2 drops of rose water, and turn the heat off. Keep it warm.
steps.visualCue: The syrup is slightly thicker and slightly sticky on the spoon, but still runs freely, and it smells of cardamom
steps.cameraCheck: The syrup dripping off a spoon in a thin stream
steps.videoShot: Spoon lifting syrup and letting it run back into the pan.
steps.watchOut: Cooking it to a thick, stringy syrup; a thick syrup will not soak into the jamuns, so they stay dry in the middle. If it gets thick, add 1 tbsp hot water and stir.
steps.funFact: "Gulab" in the name comes from the Persian word for rose water (Wikipedia).

steps.title: Shape two smooth balls
steps.text: Grease your palms with a drop of ghee or oil, split the dough into 2 equal pieces and roll each into a ball about 2.5 cm across, with no cracks.
steps.tip: Make the balls small. They will swell to about double in size in the syrup.
steps.visualCue: Two glossy, crack-free balls the size of a small marble or large grape
steps.cameraCheck: Two smooth balls on a plate
steps.videoShot: Palms rolling a ball until it is smooth.
steps.watchOut: Cracks on the surface, which open up in the oil and make the jamun fall apart; if a ball cracks, add a drop of milk to your palm and roll it again until it is smooth.

steps.title: Heat the oil
steps.text: Pour 150 ml oil into the kadai and heat it on low for 3-4 minutes. Test with a pinch of dough.
steps.visualCue: The test pinch sinks, then slowly rises with a few tiny bubbles around it, without browning at once
steps.cameraCheck: The test piece of dough in the oil
steps.videoShot: A pinch of dough sinking and rising in the oil.
steps.watchOut: Hot oil, which browns the outside while leaving the centre raw; if the test pinch rises and browns instantly, turn the heat down and wait 2 minutes.

steps.title: Slide in the balls
steps.text: Lower both balls into the oil with a spoon and leave them for 30 seconds without touching them.
steps.visualCue: The balls sink, then float up slowly with a light, steady fizz
steps.cameraCheck: The two balls in the oil
steps.watchOut: Moving them right away, which can break them; wait until they have floated and set.

steps.title: Fry on low, turning gently
steps.text: Fry for 6-8 minutes, turning them slowly all the time with the slotted spoon, until they are deep golden-brown all over (est.).
steps.visualCue: Colour goes from pale yellow to an even deep golden-brown, and the balls swell a little and feel springy when nudged
steps.cameraCheck: The two fried balls, even golden-brown, in the oil
steps.videoShot: The balls turning slowly in the oil, changing colour.
steps.watchOut: Dark spots from too-high heat, or balls that stay pale and soak up oil on too-low heat; keep the oil gently bubbling, and turn the flame up or down in small steps.

steps.title: Drain briefly
steps.text: Lift the balls with the slotted spoon and let the oil drip for 20-30 seconds.
steps.visualCue: The surface looks matt and dry, with a deep brown colour
steps.cameraCheck: The balls on the spoon above the kadai
steps.videoShot: Slotted spoon lifting the balls with oil dripping off.
steps.watchOut: Draining for too long, since the crust cools and then does not soak the syrup well; move them on to the syrup while they are still hot.

steps.title: Soak in warm syrup
steps.text: Re-warm the syrup if it has gone cold, so that it is warm (comfortable to touch, not boiling), and slide in the balls.
steps.visualCue: The balls sink into the syrup and a few tiny bubbles come up as they start to soak
steps.cameraCheck: The balls in the warm syrup
steps.videoShot: Balls sliding into the syrup in a bowl.
steps.watchOut: Boiling-hot syrup or cold syrup. Very hot syrup can shrink or break the jamuns; cold syrup does not soak in. If the syrup is cold, warm it gently for 1 minute and cool for 2 minutes before adding.

steps.title: Rest in the syrup
steps.text: Cover and leave for 2 hours (Hebbar's Kitchen), turning the jamuns once after an hour.
steps.visualCue: After soaking the balls look swollen, about double their size, glossy and soft, and sink slightly when pressed with a spoon
steps.videoShot: A spoon pressing a jamun, which springs back softly.
steps.watchOut: Cutting the rest short, which leaves a hard, pale core; cut one open at 1 hour and, if the centre is white and dry, let it soak for another hour.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Place 2 jamuns in a small bowl with 1-2 tbsp of the syrup.
steps.visualCue: Two glossy, dark-brown jamuns sitting in a shallow pool of syrup
steps.videoShot: A spoon splitting a jamun to show the soft, even inside.
steps.watchOut: Adding a lot of extra syrup, since it adds sugar without adding any taste; take only 1-2 tbsp.

reasons: a deep-fried dessert soaked in sugar syrup: about 28 g of added sugar in 2 pieces (over the 25 g limit), about 17 g fat with about 7.8 g saturated fat, almost no fibre, and refined flour. In its favour: it has some protein (about 9 g), calcium (about 28% of the day) and B12 from the milk powder, and sodium is low. Restaurant pieces are often larger and are soaked longer, so a sweeter, higher-calorie portion is likely (est.).

researchRating.basis: one of India's best-known and most-loved festival sweets (Swiggy's own blog and press report it as a most-ordered dessert), published by many recipe sites and blogs. Points off because first attempts often crack or turn hard, and it is very sweet. Recipe-site star counts were not checked this run. Platform dish ratings were not used.

storage: Keep in the syrup in a closed container; fridge-safe for about 3-4 days (not source-checked this run). Freezing is not recommended (the syrup-soaked texture changes; not source-checked). To reheat, warm 30 seconds in the microwave or in a little warm syrup in a pan on low heat.
leftoverRemix: Gulab jamun with ice cream or crumble. Chop 1 leftover jamun and serve over vanilla ice cream, or warm the pieces and spoon over plain curd with a few chopped nuts.
burnOff: about 5.4 km of running (375 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 7.5 km of brisk walking (about 1 h 30 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.).

navratri.reason: maida (refined wheat flour) is a grain flour avoided in most vrat rule sets, and baking soda is often avoided too; a vrat version would be a different dish (assumption: the common rule set; not source-checked this run; families differ)

ekadashi.reason: grain flour (maida) is avoided on Ekadashi under the common rule set (not source-checked this run; families differ)

jain.reason: no roots, onion, garlic, meat, fish, egg or honey in the recipe

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; a sweet, fried bite that is a common iftar sweet, but very high in sugar (about 28 g added) and fat, so keep to 2 pieces and avoid it at sehri

jain.reason: milk powder, maida, ghee, sugar, cardamom and rose water only; no onion, garlic, potato or any root vegetable, no egg, no honey (families differ on some sugars)

vegan.reason: milk powder, ghee and milk are dairy; established vegan versions use flours and nuts instead (see Vegan variant), which makes a different dough

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian recipe with no meat or egg

sattvik.reason: the recipe has no onion or garlic

glutenFree.reason: maida (refined wheat flour) 8 g is the gluten source; replace it with a gluten-free flour such as the coconut or almond flour used in established gluten-free versions (see Gluten-free variant)

dairyFree.reason: milk powder 30 g, ghee 3 g and milk 20 ml are dairy; only the flour-based dairy-free versions work (see Dairy-free variant)

variants.reason: Main recipe already Jain (no onion, garlic, roots, egg or honey).
